messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 60
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Warehouse Worker
- Trauma Type: Military
- Pcl5: 62

The first time I met him, he was still wearing his work boots, the laces caked with the fine grey dust of the warehouse floor. He is sixty years old, a broad-shouldered man named Karl, and he has spent the last thirty years stacking pallets and driving a forklift. He tells me this is the longest he has ever held a job. He says this with a kind of flat pride, as if surviving the monotony is its own kind of medal.

He does not talk about the war. Not at first. He tells me about his girlfriend, Lena, and how she nags him about his sleep. He tells me about the ache in his lower back that has been with him since his twenties. He tells me about the shift manager who is half his age and talks to him like he is slow. But eventually, in the third session, he stops. He looks at the carpet for a long time, and then he tells me about the bridge.

It was 1968. He was nineteen. He was a machine gunner on a transport truck in a convoy moving through a valley. He remembers the heat, the dust, the way the air tasted like diesel and sweat. He remembers the joke the driver told just before the world ended. Then the RPG hit the truck in front of them. He watched the men he had shared breakfast with become a smear of light and metal. He does not describe the sound. He just says, “It was very loud. And then it wasn’t.”

He was pulled from the wreckage of his own truck by a medic. He does not remember the medic’s face. He remembers the blood on his own hands, and that he could not stop his hands from shaking. For fifty-two years, he has not stopped shaking. He learned to hide it. He learned to hold his coffee mug with two hands. He learned to keep his fists in his pockets during the morning safety briefings at the warehouse.

Karl lives in a state of constant, low-grade hypervigilance. He cannot stand having his back to a door. In the warehouse, he always positions his forklift so he can see the main aisle. When a pallet drops unexpectedly—a crash of wood and shrink wrap—his entire body seizes. He tells me he feels his heart “hit his ribs like a trapped bird.” He will then spend the next hour scanning the rafters, looking for the sniper he knows is not there.

The nightmares are the worst. They are not memories, he says. They are *the same thing*. He wakes up in his bed in the apartment he shares with Lena, drenched in sweat, convinced he is back in the valley. He has punched the wall twice. He has thrown a lamp. Lena sleeps in the guest room now. He does not blame her. He says he is a ghost haunting his own life.

At work, he is reliable but silent. His coworkers think he is antisocial. They do not know that the loud music on the warehouse radio—the classic rock station—makes him flinch because it drowns out the sound of approaching footsteps. They do not know that when the new kid sneaks up behind him to ask a question, Karl nearly swings. He stopped that reflex years ago, but the intention, the raw animal fury, is still there. It lives just under his skin.

He avoids crowds. He avoids the Fourth of July. He avoids war movies, news reports about veterans, and the sound of helicopters. The warehouse is a safe place because it is predictable. The same boxes. The same aisles. The same mind-numbing routine. He tells me the routine is what keeps him from falling apart. He tells me he is not sick. He is just tired. So very, very tired. He looks at me with eyes that have been looking for an exit for half a century, and he asks if I think he will ever feel safe again.
